GERMANY NGO FUNDING MAP
Public Interest Data Project

What this dataset is

A compiled dataset from 13 official public primary sources documenting German public funding flows to NGOs. Each record has a confidence_level (verified/estimated/inferred) and a traceable source_url. This dataset documents funding flows — it does not attribute conduct or intent to any organization.

Acceptable use

  • Journalism, academic research, public policy analysis
  • Personal, educational, and non-profit use
  • Reproduction with attribution to primary sources

Prohibited use

  • Attributing criminal, fraudulent, or immoral conduct to any organization based solely on this dataset
  • Presenting data as “exclusive” when the primary source is publicly available
  • Combining with personal data without appropriate legal basis

Key limitations

  • 92% of OECD CRS records use generic channel names — no individual organization names. This is a documented finding about Germany's reporting architecture, not a data error.
  • Political foundations (~€700M/year): federal funding known, redistribution to local partners is opaque
  • Churches (Caritas/Diakonie): ~€1.5B/year redistribution is private, zero coverage
  • 13 of 16 German states have no public subsidy database

License

CC BY-SA 4.0 — You must cite primary sources for any specific claims. Derivative datasets must use the same license.

Pressekodex note

This dataset provides what responsible data journalism requires: traceable primary sources, documented limitations, confidence levels per record, and factual restraint. Statistical patterns are documented for further investigation, never as accusations.

Your Taxes

Where every £ of your tax actually goes. Methodology ↗

£0£100k£200k+
Don't know your band? Check on gov.uk ↗
How this is calculated
  • Income Tax + NI: exact per HMRC bands for 2024-25 (rUK or Scotland).
  • VAT + duties: estimated from ONS decile consumption data — the number depends on spending habits, this shows the typical figure for your income level.
  • Council Tax: exact from MHCLG 2024-25 tables (all-in: billing authority + county + GLA + police + fire + parish).
  • Borrowing: UK gov. borrowed £139B in 2022-23 (~£4,900/household). This figure is the same for every household regardless of salary — what the state added to the national debt on your behalf this year, to be repaid by future taxes. It does not shrink when your salary grows; the Sankey link just looks smaller in proportion because your own tax contribution is larger.
  • Spending attribution: government doesn't earmark taxes — all revenue pools in the Consolidated Fund. This visualisation shows pro-rata "for every £ spent by central gov, where a £ of yours would fit."
  • Your council's share: real per-council grant data from MHCLG Revenue Outturn.

Not included: dividend/savings tax · self-employed NIC Class 2/4 · pension contributions (your savings, not tax) · student loan (not a tax) · employer NIC · corporation tax incidence.

Sources · every number above is traceable
Income Tax & NI bands HMRC 2024-25 ↗ data/uk/fiscal/uk_tax_bands.json
VAT & indirect tax by decile ONS ETB 2022 ↗ data/uk/fiscal/uk_indirect_tax_by_decile.json
Council Tax (all-in, 328 councils) MHCLG 2024-25 ↗ data/uk/fiscal/uk_council_tax_2024.json
Central spending composition HMT OSCAR II ↗ data/uk/uk_budget_tree_2024.json
Per-council grant share MHCLG RO5 ↗ data/uk/local_authorities/council_spend_lookup_2024.json
Public borrowing (PSNB) OBR March 2024 EFO ↗ data/uk/fiscal/uk_public_finance_totals.json
Every committed data file has a SHA256 you can verify against our public repo ↗. Open a methodology question? File an issue ↗.

Where does every £ come from?

Budget Galaxy's taxpayer view combines six public datasets with a calculator that reconciles everything to HMRC-published totals. Every number you see is auditable in our public repo.

The four taxes we compute directly

TaxSourcePrecision
Income TaxHMRC 2024-25 bands (rUK + Scotland)Exact
NI Class 1 (employee)HMRC 2024-25 thresholds (8% / 2%)Exact
VAT + indirect dutiesONS "Effects of Taxes & Benefits" decile consumptionEstimated — scales with your disposable income decile
Council TaxMHCLG 2024-25 area council tax tables (all-in: billing authority + county/GLA + police + fire + parish)Exact

How your £ flows through government

Government does not earmark taxes — every pound enters the Consolidated Fund and gets spent from there. We visualise pro-rata: "for every £ spent by central gov, where a £ of yours would fit."

  1. Your IT + NI + VAT flows from HMRC buckets into the Consolidated Fund.
  2. The Consolidated Fund distributes across 10 spending groups (Health, DWP, Education, Defence, Debt Interest, Local Gov grants, Scotland/Wales/NI block grants, Transport, HMRC ops, Other) in proportion to HM Treasury's uk_budget_tree_2024.json.
  3. Your Council Tax goes directly to your billing authority — not via the Consolidated Fund.
  4. Your council's share of the central "Local Gov grants" pot is computed from real MHCLG Revenue Outturn data — your council's grant ÷ all-councils grant. So if your council is Birmingham (big city, ~2% of all council grants), that 2% of the central grant bucket flows to them.
  5. That total reaching your council (Council Tax + grant share) is then split across the services your council spends on — Adult Social Care, Education, Children's Social Care, Public Health, Transport, Housing, etc. — in proportion to their RS_*_net_exp figures.

Government borrowing — why it's a separate node

UK government spent more than it received in 2022-23 — £139 billion more. That difference is borrowed. Divided evenly across the UK's ~28.4 million households, every household gets a £4,902 share of the debt added this year. This figure is the same for every household regardless of salary.

In the Sankey, borrowing appears as a separate red source funding the Consolidated Fund — on top of what your taxes cover. It will be repaid by future taxes. Because future taxes are progressive, a high earner's future repayment obligation is larger than a low earner's — but the this-year-added figure is the same flat per-household amount.

What is NOT included

  • Self-employed NIC (Class 2 & 4)
  • Dividend tax & savings tax
  • Capital gains tax (event-based)
  • Stamp Duty Land Tax (event-based — only on property purchase)
  • Employer NIC (not your direct liability)
  • Corporation Tax incidence on consumers (disputed)
  • Pension contributions (these are your savings, not tax)
  • Student loan repayments (not a tax)

Audit trail

Every raw file is committed to the public Budget Galaxy repository with a SHA256 hash in data/uk/fiscal/SOURCES_TAX.md. Re-run any of our parsing scripts in scripts/ to reproduce the JSON files the frontend loads.

Known limitations (v1)

  • England-only council data — Scotland/Wales/NI have different systems; coming v1.1.
  • Decile VAT estimate is ONS FY2017-18; ratios are stable year-to-year.
  • Precepts to county/GLA/police/fire are collapsed into the billing authority total.
  • PSNB uses 2022-23 outturn (£139bn); 2023-24 and 2024-25 forecasts land in subsequent OBR releases.

About Budget Galaxy

A reference tool for public spending across four countries. Updated April 2026.
Methodology

Budget Galaxy aggregates UK public spending and tax data from the official primary sources. Every number traces back to a named file we committed with a SHA256 hash.

Central government spending
  • HM Treasury OSCAR II: ~55 departments, executive agencies and bodies. The 2023 OSCAR edition was reprocessed to correct a £114B NHS artifact that would otherwise double-count health spending. Same n/a-trust artifact also removed for 2020-2022.
  • NHS: trust-level operating cost breakdowns for 206 provider trusts (118 acute, 45 mental health, 18 community, 15 specialist, 10 ambulance), with workforce and cost-type metadata where published. NHS commissioner (ICB) and provider (trust) values are netted against each other to avoid double-counting.
Tax receipts & bands
  • HMRC tax receipts 2005-2024 (annual bulletin): full breakdown by tax type — Income Tax, NI, VAT, Corporation Tax, fuel duty, stamp taxes, IHT, CGT, APD, IPT, duties and more.
  • Income Tax + NI bands for rUK and Scotland, fiscal years 2017-18 through 2024-25, from HMRC's "Rates and thresholds for employers" and Scottish Government publications.
  • VAT & indirect tax estimation: ONS "Effects of Taxes and Benefits" decile consumption shares.
Local government
  • 401 English local authorities from MHCLG Revenue Outturn (2017/18-2024/25), plus 32 Scottish councils from gov.scot for council tax bands.
  • 19 English councils with supplier-level spend parsed from their own published registers and classified into MHCLG service categories. An additional 7 police and fire authorities are covered as separate entities.
  • Population data: ONS mid-2023 local authority estimates for per-capita analysis.
Borrowing
  • OBR Historical Public Finances Database: Public Sector Net Borrowing (PSNB) and Net Debt (PSND) from 2000-01 through 2022-23, with nominal GDP for % calculations.

The full data pipeline is in the project repository. Every number on this site can be traced back to a specific line in a specific source file. See the council spend source manifest and the tax data source manifest for the three-layer audit trail: live landing pages, Wayback Machine snapshots, and SHA256-hashed raw files committed to git.

What went wrong

Public spending data has gaps, inconsistencies, and quirks that most transparency tools hide. Budget Galaxy documents them here because they matter for how you read the numbers.

Birmingham City Council is absent from the 2023-24 tree. Birmingham issued a Section 114 notice in September 2023, which disrupted their MHCLG submission pipeline. Their public spend register (City Observatory) uses a rolling 24-month window that has since purged 2023-24 transactions. We tried six alternative sources and recovered nothing. The 2024-25 data exists but cannot be injected because Birmingham has no node in the MHCLG-derived tree for that year.
Cornwall’s supplier totals are under review. Cornwall’s MHCLG net current expenditure (£1.0B) is consistent with other unitary authorities. But the supplier-level spend derived from Cornwall’s raw CSV sums to approximately £6.2B — roughly 6x the MHCLG operating value, compared to a ratio closer to 1.1x for other councils. The most likely explanation is that Cornwall’s “Net Amount” column includes capital expenditure and internal transfers alongside operating spend. Until this is reconciled, treat Cornwall’s supplier figures as an upper bound.
NHS commissioner and provider spending overlap. NHS Integrated Care Boards commission services from NHS Trusts. Summing ICB commissioning and Trust operating costs directly would double-count the same money. Budget Galaxy nets these values against each other. If you compare to a source that doesn’t do this netting, expect your totals to be larger than ours.
OSCAR 2023 had a £114B health artifact. The 2023 edition of HM Treasury’s OSCAR II dataset contained a £114B discrepancy in health spending that appears to be an accounting-transition artifact from the shift to OSCAR II. We removed it. Our 2023 UK total is therefore lower than a naive OSCAR 2023 sum by approximately that amount. The same "n/a" NHS Trusts sub-bucket pattern exists in the 2020, 2021, and 2022 trees and was removed in the same way.
Local government depth is England-only. Each of the four UK nations has its total public spending captured at the devolved administration level (Scottish Government £36.84B, Welsh Assembly Government £23.90B, Northern Ireland Executive £33.21B), but only England has a council-by-council breakdown inside Local Government (England). The reason is regulatory: England’s 401 local authorities all report to MHCLG in a standardized Revenue Outturn format. Scotland’s 32 councils report to the Accounts Commission, Wales’s 22 to Welsh Government, and Northern Ireland’s 11 districts to DoF NI — three separate data regimes with different schemas. Integrating them would require three independent pipelines carefully netted against the devolved government totals already captured, to avoid double-counting. For now, treat Scotland, Wales, and NI local spending as aggregated inside their devolved administration node, not broken down by council. The 19 councils with supplier-level detail are also all English for the same reason.

When additional countries are enabled (US / Germany / France / Brazil are next on the roadmap), each will get its own gap-disclosure section below.

Enrichment coverage & quality (audit 2026-04-27)

When you click any node in Explore & Compare or Budget Galaxy, you see a contextual "About this programme" panel. The content comes from four layers of increasing quality, documented here honestly because quality varies.

The four tiers
  • Tier A — Hand-curated (4,199 entries · 15,245 source citations). Written across multiple sprints of research against official publishers — DWP Stat-Xplore, HMRC Annual Report, NHS England TAC, ONS, IFS, OBR, NAO, House of Commons Library briefings, NHS provider Trust ARAs, council ARAs, COFOG aggregates. Each entry has a description, beneficiary count, legal basis, 8–12 key stats, recent-change notes, and 4–6 source citations as {publisher, title, url} dicts. Caveat: the underlying research was prepared by LLM agents using their training data (through early 2026). Numbers are cross-checked against our own tree JSON by scripts/verify_enrichment.py. Coverage of the 8–12 stats / 4–6 sources / 3–6 related-links contract floor: 86% / 41% / 71% as of 2026-04-27 — the 59% below source floor are early-sprint entries pending re-audit.
  • Tier B — Imported (2,225 nodes). Pre-existing enrichment content in the repo: program_enrichment.json (779 compact entries, schema year / description / beneficiaries) and enrichment_top50.json (651 rich entries, adding legal basis / notes / OSCAR category). These cover 25% of the tree. Caveat: most of this content was LLM-drafted at an earlier stage and not re-audited. The 2026-04-20 audit flagged 11 top-level departments with incorrect founding years (Home Office listed as founded in 2024 vs actual 1782, MoJ as 2024 vs 2007, etc.). The frontend now suppresses any Established: 2024 field coming from this layer as a sentinel for "unknown" — but other factual details in these 2,225 entries are not individually verified.
  • Tier C — Procedural (~1,500 council + council-service nodes). Generated at render time from our own data: _top_suppliers metadata joined with ONS mid-2023 local-authority populations (345 England + Wales authorities) to show population, spend per resident, tier-average comparator, top supplier, supplier concentration, and top purposes. 69% of councils in the tree match an ONS population row; the other 31% are police & crime commissioners, fire authorities and combined authorities — they don't have population rows by design (they serve multiple councils' populations combined). Those still get Tier D.
  • Tier D — Contextual fallback (every remaining node). For any node that doesn't match A/B/C, the frontend generates a card showing the ancestor chain ("part of X, part of Y"), the node's rank among siblings, and the neighbours immediately above and below it in size. Purely from the tree; zero external data needed. This guarantees every single node in the UK tree shows some context — no bare "MEH" card anywhere.
What we know is still weak
  • Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland councils get Tier D (not C) because ONS publishes England & Wales population data only; SG/WG/NISRA equivalents are not yet loaded.
  • Combined Authorities (GLA, Greater Manchester, West Midlands etc.) get Tier C via a heuristic but the "tier comparator" line uses the wrong reference group. Cosmetic, not factual.
  • Most Tier A source citations point at a publisher + title but not a clickable URL. The publications are all real and findable, but users can't one-click.
  • The Tier B 2,225-entry layer has not been individually fact-checked. A user may encounter a date or figure that's out of sync. Please file an issue — the verifier script (scripts/verify_enrichment.py) is kept in the repo to make each flag quick to reproduce.

The verifier is reproducible: py scripts/verify_enrichment.py writes data/uk/_enrichment_audit.json with per-entry flags for tree-match, scope discrepancy, missing URLs, and suspicious founding years. It runs in under a second.

Audit trail — the 4-layer verifiability model

Whenever Budget Galaxy cites a number, we want you to be able to prove it came from where we claim it came from — even if the publisher reorganises their site or pulls the page down. Four redundant layers per citation:

  1. Live source URL — the publisher's own page (gov.uk, nhs.uk, ONS, etc). Fragile: UK government reorganises URLs constantly (DWP routes changed in 2024, BEIS split into DESNZ/DSIT/DBT in Feb 2023).
  2. Wayback Machine snapshot — web.archive.org/web/<ts>/<url>. Permanent HTML capture taken when we cited the page. Click "archive ↗" next to any source.
  3. Archive.org file mirror — for raw data files (CSVs, PDFs, ZIPs), we upload a permanent copy to the Internet Archive collection budget-galaxy-uk-councils-2024 via their S3 API. Currently used for the 161 council spend datasets (~2.1 GB).
  4. Captured-at timestamp — ISO 8601 timestamp on every archived citation, so the audit is dated and reproducible.

Coverage 2026-04-27: council spend lookup 161/166 (97%) all four layers. Budget tree enrichment 4,199 entries / 15,245 citations — layer 2 (Wayback) being archived now via scripts/archive_enrichment_sources.js (~1 hour run with authenticated IA S3 keys, ~100 req/min). Layers 1 + 4 already at 100% in the JSON. Layer 3 only relevant for raw data files (not URL-based publisher pages).

Who built this and why

Budget Galaxy is built and maintained by an independent developer. The project is open and every number is traceable to an official source.

The project exists because public spending data is technically published but practically unreadable. Central government datasets are scattered across official portals, tax receipts are in monthly ODS bulletins, local government data is fragmented across 400+ councils, and nothing connects your specific tax bill to the services it funds. Budget Galaxy connects all of it for the UK; more countries are being onboarded with the same depth.

The data, the pipeline, and the full source are in the project repository.

Über German Budget Galaxy

Was ist das?

Eine interaktive Visualisierung der gesamten öffentlichen Ausgaben in Deutschland, den USA, Frankreich und Großbritannien. Allein für Deutschland: €2,3 Billionen — aufgeschlüsselt nach Bundeshaushalt, Sozialversicherungen (GKV, Rente, Arbeitslosenversicherung, Pflege, Unfallversicherung), 16 Bundesländern und Kommunen.

Jede Kugel, die Sie sehen, stellt eine reale Haushaltsposition dar. Die Größe ist proportional zum Betrag. Klicken Sie auf eine Kugel, um zu sehen, was sich darin befindet. Zoomen Sie hinein für Details. Jeder Euro, Dollar und jedes Pfund ist einer offiziellen Quelle zuordenbar.

Warum gibt es das?

Der Bundeshaushalt ist öffentlich. Er wird jährlich vom Bundesministerium der Finanzen veröffentlicht. Jeder kann ihn einsehen.

Aber „öffentlich“ ist nicht dasselbe wie „zugänglich“. Die offiziellen Daten verteilen sich auf tausende Seiten von Einzelplänen in einem Format, das für parlamentarische Verfahren konzipiert ist, nicht für öffentliches Verständnis. Zu wissen, dass €44,8 Mrd. in die Rentenversicherung fließen, ist nicht dasselbe wie es neben den €47 Mio. für den Bundespräsidenten zu sehen.

Dieses Projekt macht die Struktur sichtbar. Nicht um für mehr oder weniger Ausgaben in irgendeinem Bereich zu argumentieren, sondern um jedem — Bürger, Journalist, Student, Forscher — ein unmittelbares, intuitives Verständnis davon zu geben, wohin das Geld fließt.

Drei Werkzeuge

Budget Galaxy

Der visuelle Einstiegspunkt. Eine zoombare Kreispackungsvisualisierung, in der jedes Ministerium eine Kugel ist und innerhalb jedes Ministeriums Kapitel und Titel verschachtelt sind. Die größte Kugel — Arbeit und Soziales mit €175,7 Mrd. — ist unmöglich zu übersehen. Das ist der Punkt.

Budget Explorer

Das analytische Werkzeug. Navigieren Sie die Haushaltshierarchie mit einem Brotkrumenpfad. Jede Ebene zeigt eine Aufschlüsselung mit Prozenten, Ausgabenartanalyse und angereichertem Kontext — wer profitiert, wie viel pro Person, wie Deutschland international vergleicht.

Budget Evolution

Die historische Ansicht. Zehn Jahre Haushaltsdaten (2015–2024), die zeigen, wie sich die Ausgaben verändert haben. Der COVID-Anstieg. Die Zeitenwende in der Verteidigung. Die Explosion der Zinskosten.

Datenquellen

Deutschland: Bundeshaushalt über bundeshaushalt.de, Sozialversicherungsdaten von GKV-Spitzenverband, DRV Bund, Bundesagentur für Arbeit; Länderhaushalte und Kommunalfinanzen über Destatis. USA: USAspending.gov. Frankreich: data.gouv.fr (PLF). UK: HM Treasury OSCAR.

Anreicherungsdaten (Empfängerzahlen, internationale Vergleiche) stammen von offiziellen Statistiken der jeweiligen Behörden: Deutsche Rentenversicherung, Bundesagentur für Arbeit, OECD, NATO, Destatis und andere.

Einschränkungen

• Der Bundeshaushalt zeigt den Soll-Haushalt, nicht die tatsächlichen Ausgaben (Ist).

• Außeretatmäßige Posten wie das Sondervermögen Bundeswehr (€100 Mrd.) und der Klima- und Transformationsfonds sind nicht enthalten.

• Die Gesamtdarstellung (€2,3 Bio.) enthält Überschneidungen zwischen Ebenen (z.B. Bundeszuschüsse zur Rentenversicherung). Der konsolidierte Gesamtbetrag ist niedriger.

• Anreicherungsdaten sind näherungsweise und aus verschiedenen Berichtszeiträumen (meist 2023–2024).

Jeder Euro, der von Bürgerinnen und Bürgern erhoben wird, sollte verständlich sein für diese Bürger. Nicht in parlamentarischen Formaten eingeschlossen. Nicht hinter Fachjargon versteckt. Sichtbar, erkundbar und vergleichbar — das ist, was dieses Werkzeug bietet.

What this dataset is

This is a compiled dataset from 13 official public primary sources documenting German public funding flows to non-governmental organizations. It covers the period 2010–2025 and contains 528,000+ records.

Every record carries a confidence_level field (verified, estimated, or inferred) and a traceable source_url linking to the original primary source. The dataset documents funding flows — it does not attribute conduct, intent, or wrongdoing to any organization.

Statistical patterns in the dataset are detected by automated queries. They indicate data points that warrant further investigation by qualified journalists or researchers. They are not accusations.
